meta_home_title: EpiDetective — Open tools for reading health evidence
meta_home_desc: Free tools that let you explore the published evidence on what causes cancer and other major chronic diseases. Built by a cancer epidemiologist at IARC/WHO.
meta_explorer_desc: See which exposures have been linked to which cancers, and how strong the evidence is for each link. Built on the WHO's IARC Monographs.
home_h1: Translating epidemiological evidence for a healthier world
home_audience: For the curious public, patients, doctors, journalists, and the people who write health policy.
home_lede: EpiDetective builds free tools that let you explore published health research for yourself.
inst_h2: Two are open now. More are being built.
inst_t1_desc: See which exposures have been linked to which cancers, and how strong the evidence is behind each link. It is built on the IARC Monographs, the World Health Organization's review of what can cause cancer. Start from a cancer, start from an exposure, or open the whole map.
inst_t2_desc: Which risk factors have been linked to heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, dementia, cancer and other major chronic conditions — and how strong the evidence is behind each link, including where it is genuinely contested. Pull the network apart to see how the risk factors group together.
about_h2: Built by a cancer epidemiologist who works with this data every day.
about_p1: I am Wenxin Wan, a postdoctoral researcher at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the World Health Organization's cancer agency, based in Lyon, France.
about_p2: I obtained my MSc in Epidemiology from the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom, and my PhD from Utrecht University in the Netherlands, where I studied how exposures at work and in the environment shape cancer risk at the population level. Part of that work provided new evidence on the causal relationship between benzene and lung cancer, and was covered by The New York Times.
about_p3: My daily work at IARC revolves around large international cohorts: millions of people followed over many years so that the risk factors causally linked to disease can be identified. I lead the analysis and coordinate the project for OPICO, the international opioid cohort consortium, which brings ten cohorts from three continents together to ask what cancer risk long-term opioid use may carry; and I serve as scientific advisor to the Lung Cancer Cohort Consortium (LC3), helping carry the evidence built up by occupational-exposure research into lung cancer screening for populations worldwide.
about_p4: I have spent years helping to produce this kind of evidence myself, yet far too little of it ever reaches ordinary people — the very people the research was meant to protect. That has frustrated me for a long time. A finding that stays inside the literature has done less than half its job. Closing that distance is worth every bit of effort we can give it, and that is why I created this site.

foot_affiliation: EpiDetective is a personal project by Wenxin Wan, produced in a personal capacity. It carries no endorsement from the International Agency for Research on Cancer or the World Health Organization, and the views expressed here belong to the author alone. The underlying scientific sources are cited so that anyone can check them independently.
foot_disclaimer: EpiDetective publishes tools for reading evidence about whole populations. They show patterns across large groups of people. For anything concerning your own health, speak to a doctor. Each tool lists its own sources.

exp_h1: Some exposures cause cancer. Some might. Telling them apart is the whole job.
exp_lede: Every mark behind this text is real: 185 exposures, 68 types of cancer, and the 469 links the World Health Organization's cancer agency has recorded between them.
exp_whatsin_h2: The exposures the IARC has linked to a cancer, graded by how certain the evidence is.
exp_bar1_note: Studies in people agree closely enough to rule out chance, bias and other explanations. This is the strongest conclusion the IARC draws.
exp_bar2_note: A causal reading of the association is credible, but chance, bias or confounding cannot yet be ruled out. The question remains open, and more research may settle it either way.
exp_reads_h2: Three limits of this map, worth knowing before you read it.
exp_read1_h3: Something that can cause cancer may still have had nothing to do with yours.
exp_read1_p: A Group 1 classification means an exposure can cause cancer under some conditions. How much, for how long, at what age, and which genes you carry all stand between that finding and any one person.
exp_read2_h3: A missing link may only mean nobody has looked hard enough yet.
exp_read2_p: The map records what has been studied and reviewed. Many gaps come from limited research funding or short follow-up time, so an empty space here is weak evidence of safety.
exp_read3_h3: This map describes populations, and cannot judge any single case.
exp_read3_p: If you are living with a cancer diagnosis, the people treating you know things about your case that no population map contains. Bring your questions to them.
exp_cta_h2: Start from a cancer. Start from an exposure. Or open the whole map.
exp_cta_lede: Free, in ten languages. Drag, zoom, and focus on any part of the network.
exp_cta_source: Source: IARC Monographs, "Classifications by cancer site", Volumes 1–141 (last update 18 May 2026), adapted from Schubauer-Berigan et al., JNCI Monographs 2026. This tool identifies hazards across whole populations. For anything concerning your own health, speak to a doctor.

meta_games_title: Cancer awareness games — sun, lung and breast — EpiDetective
meta_games_desc: Three free browser games about cancer prevention: Sol & the UV Shield Quest (sun safety, ages 6 to 12), The Lung Detective (what causes lung cancer, ages 10 to 16) and A Town of 1,000 (breast cancer in a town followed for forty years, ages 14 and up). No download, nothing collected.
games_sub: A side-scrolling adventure that teaches children how to enjoy the sun without harming their skin.
games_p1: Most skin cancers are caused by ultraviolet radiation, and the habits that prevent them are learned young. In this game Sol runs, jumps and collects sun stars across five regions, from a grassy meadow to a snowy mountain. Along the way Sol picks up a broad-brimmed hat and SPF 30+ sunscreen, loses the sunscreen after a swim, and reaches checkpoints where a quiz question must be answered before the path opens again.
games_p2: The questions cover what the UV Index means, when protection matters (UV 3 and above), why shade, clothing and sunscreen work best together, how sand, water and snow reflect UV, and why tanning beds should be avoided. Wrong answers are never punished: Sol is nudged back with a hint and a laugh. The game runs in your browser, works on a phone, and collects no data. It is in English.
games_fact_questions: questions in the bank, 5 per run
games_step1: Press Play. On a keyboard, move with A D or ← → and jump with Space. On a phone, use the on-screen buttons. A game controller works too.
games_step2: Collect sun coins and the nine hidden sun stars. Some platforms move, some fall, so keep moving.
games_step3: Watch the UV Index in the top bar. It changes from region to region, and drops when Sol stands in shade.
games_step4: At each checkpoint, read the question and jump up beneath one of the three answer blocks. The right answer opens the gate; a wrong one gives a hint and another try.
games_step5: Press <kbd>R</kbd> to restart. The cog opens the settings: voice narration, high contrast, a dyslexia-friendly font, larger text, game speed and touch-control size.
games_regions_h: The five regions and their UV Index
games_fine: The game uses an original character and artwork. Its source is open at github.com/Wenxin-Wan/sun-safety-adventure. The sun-safety advice follows the European Code Against Cancer and WHO guidance on UV protection.

games_g1_desc: A platform adventure about sun safety for children aged 6 to 12. Five regions, a quiz at each checkpoint, and a shield kit of hat, cover-up, shade and sunscreen to assemble along the way.
games_over_lede: Each game teaches one part of cancer prevention through play. They run in the browser, collect no data, and show the source behind everything they say. Choose one to see how it is played and what it teaches.
games_g2_sub: An investigation across a flat, a street and a building yard, in which every clue is filed the way IARC files evidence.
games_g2_p1: Smoking causes most lung cancers, and stopping helps at whatever age it happens. That is the first finding in the case file, and the rest of the investigation builds on it. The player searches three scenes, a flat, a street and a building yard, and turns up twelve clues. Each has to be filed the way IARC files evidence: a known cause of lung cancer (Group 1), a probable cause (Group 2A), or something with no evidence behind it. The real hazards can then be fixed, and a clean-air score rises with each one.
games_g2_p2: The clues cover second-hand smoke; radon in the home, with a small detector game built around the WHO reference level of 100 Bq/m³; outdoor air pollution and diesel exhaust; wood smoke and high-temperature frying; and the silica dust, asbestos and welding fumes of a building site. Bitumen roofing lands in the probable group, and coffee and stress turn out to have no evidence behind them at all. Three conversations carry the argument: a flatmate who smokes only a few a day, a vape-shop owner who calls vaping harmless, and a foreman who thinks quitting after twenty years is pointless. Every clue shows its source and the official wording of the European Code Against Cancer. The game runs in your browser, works on a phone, and collects no data. It is in English.
games_g2_step1: Press Play. Use the mouse or a finger, or Tab to reach a clue and Enter to inspect it. The pulsing rings mark where the clues are.
games_g2_step2: File each clue in one of three drawers: known cause (Group 1), probable cause (Group 2A), or no evidence. A wrong drawer is greyed out and you try again; the right one opens the source and the wording of the European Code Against Cancer.
games_g2_step3: Fix the hazards that can be fixed. Each one raises the clean-air score. In the flat, the radon detector is a small game of its own: the WHO reference level is 100 Bq/m³, and WHO says national reference levels should not exceed 300.
games_g2_step4: Talk to the three people you meet: the flatmate, the vape-shop owner and the foreman. Each has a reason to doubt, and each gets the evidence, kindly.
games_g2_step5: The cog opens the settings: high contrast, larger text, wider and easier-to-read letters, and reduced motion. The report at the end shows what was filed, what was fixed and the clean-air score.
games_g2_fine: Every clue in the game cites its source. The classifications follow the IARC Monographs, the prevention wording is that of the European Code Against Cancer, and the radon reference level is the WHO's (100 Bq/m³). The finding that stopping smoking helps at any age comes from Peto and colleagues (BMJ, 2000).
games_g2_desc: An investigation game about what causes lung cancer, for ages 10 to 16. Three scenes, twelve clues to file as known cause, probable cause or no evidence, a radon detector to read, and three people to talk round.

games_g3_sub: A choices game in which a town council follows 1,000 women from their twenties to their sixties and sees, dot by dot, what prevention changes.
games_g3_p1: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, and much of what is said about preventing it rests on very little. In this game the player is the council of a town whose 1,000 women are followed from their twenties to their sixties. Each of five chapters brings two decision cards and a small effort budget to spend on them: alcohol, physical activity, weight after the menopause, breastfeeding, menopausal hormone therapy, screening. The outcome appears on an array of 1,000 dots as the number of women diagnosed with breast cancer by age 75, about 94 of 1,000 in Western Europe (GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates), and the number who die of it, about 15.
games_g3_p2: The effect sizes are modest and honest, taken from pooled studies, so a good decade of choices moves a handful of dots. Myth cards are there to be spotted: antiperspirants and underwired bras cost effort and change nothing, and a smoke-free card explains that for breast cancer the evidence on smoking is limited, whatever smoking does elsewhere in the body. The game ends with an honesty panel: these are population averages, and they predict nothing about any one woman. It runs in your browser, works on a phone, and collects no data. It is in English.
games_g3_step1: Press Play. You sit as the council of a town whose 1,000 women you will follow for forty years, one chapter for each decade of their lives.
games_g3_step2: Each chapter deals two decision cards and gives you a small effort budget. Read both cards, then spend the budget where you think it will count.
games_g3_step3: Watch the 1,000 dots. Each choice moves the number of women diagnosed by age 75, and the number who die of it, by the amount the pooled studies support. Small movements are the honest ones.
games_g3_step4: Some cards are myths. Antiperspirants and underwired bras cost effort and move nothing; the smoke-free card explains why the breast-cancer evidence for smoking is only limited.
games_g3_step5: Read the honesty panel at the end. The numbers are averages for a population like Western Europe's, and no dot stands for any one woman.
games_g3_fine: Baseline figures are for Western Europe (GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates). Effect sizes come from pooled studies of alcohol, physical activity, weight after the menopause, breastfeeding, menopausal hormone therapy and screening participation. The prevention advice follows the European Code Against Cancer.
games_g3_desc: A choices game about breast cancer prevention, for ages 14 and up. Five chapters, ten decision cards, a small effort budget, and 1,000 dots that show, honestly, how many women a town's choices spare.
